usage: 고속버스 + 타다 is the default frame; the means of transport you ride takes 을/를 or just 타고, never 으로 here
the building you depart from — 강남, 센트럴시티 등이 유명; buses use 터미널, never 역
우등(優等) = 'superior grade', 3 wide seats per row with more legroom and a higher fare; worth knowing when booking
예매(豫買) 'buy in advance' is the standard word for booking transport tickets ahead, usually on the 코버스 app
examples: 고속버스가 기차보다 싸요.
The express bus is cheaper than the train.
simple A보다 B comparison; 보다 attaches to the thing you measure against
주말이라 고속버스 표가 다 매진됐어요.
It's the weekend, so the express bus tickets are all sold out.
매진(賣盡)되다 = to sell out completely; book early on holidays
우등으로 예매하면 자리가 넓어서 훨씬 편해요.
If you book the premium one, the seats are wide so it's much more comfortable.
우등으로 uses 으로 'in the manner of'; this is why people pay extra
nuance: 고속버스 (高速 'high-speed' + 버스) is the intercity coach that runs city-to-city on the expressway with few or no stops, so Koreans habitually weigh it against three rivals: the KTX (faster, pricier), the cheaper 무궁화호 train, and 시외버스, which makes more stops and reaches smaller towns. The dividing line you must keep straight is 고속버스 vs 시외버스 — 고속버스 means nonstop expressway travel between major cities and leaves from a 고속버스 터미널, while 시외버스 zig-zags through provincial towns from a different window. It is neutral everyday vocabulary anyone uses, collocating with 타다, 예매하다, 표/자리, and 우등. The classic English-speaker pitfall is saying 고속버스역: buses board at a 터미널, and 역 belongs to trains and subways only; a second trap is reaching for 으로 ('by bus') when the natural pattern is simply 고속버스(를) 타다 or 타고 가다.

mistakes: Saying 고속버스역 — buses use 터미널, not 역 (역 is strictly for trains and subways), so it's 고속버스 터미널.

usage: used for trips to smaller cities or towns a 고속버스 doesn't reach
often shares a building with the 고속버스 terminal but has a separate ticket window
시간표 'time-table' = schedule; rural departures are sparse, so check it first
완행(緩行) 'slow-going' stops at many towns; its opposite is 직행(直行) 'direct'
examples: 그 마을은 시외버스로 가요.
You get to that village by intercity bus.
simple statement; the route a 고속버스 skips
시외버스는 정류장에 자주 서서 시간이 더 걸려요.
The intercity bus stops at stations often, so it takes more time.
서다 here = to stop/pull over; this is the trade-off vs 고속버스
시외버스 막차가 8시라서 서둘러야 해요.
The last intercity bus is at 8, so we have to hurry.
막차 (last bus) is a survival word; rural lines end early in the evening
nuance: 시외버스 (市外 'outside-the-city' + 버스) is the regional coach that covers shorter routes and makes multiple stops, so it reaches the provincial towns a 고속버스 deliberately skips. The synonym line learners must internalize is 시외버스 vs 고속버스: both are intercity buses, but 고속버스 means nonstop expressway runs between big cities, whereas 시외버스 threads through smaller places and is therefore slower — they even sell from different windows in the same terminal. Within 시외버스 there is a further split, 완행 (all-stops) vs 직행 (express/few-stops), so 직행 시외버스 can be nearly as quick as a 고속버스. It is plain, neutral vocabulary that collocates with 타다, 시간표, 막차, and 정류장. The big English-speaker pitfall is assuming buses run frequently the way they do in a city: rural 시외버스 lines may depart only a handful of times a day, so you must check the 시간표 and never count on a late return.

usage: read aloud as '케이티엑스'; Korea's flagship high-speed rail
done on the 코레일톡 (Korail Talk) app or at the station 매표소
특실(特室) 'special room' = first class, roomier; 일반실(一般室) = standard
자유석(自由席) = no assigned seat, cheaper; sit anywhere in the 자유석 cars, unlike 입석 (standing)
examples: 서울에서 부산까지 KTX로 가요.
I go from Seoul to Busan by KTX.
with a named train/vehicle, 으로/로 'by means of' is natural here, unlike with 버스+타고
KTX 표가 비싸지만 빠르니까 자주 타요.
KTX tickets are expensive but since they're fast I take it often.
captures the everyday price-vs-speed reasoning; -니까 gives the reason
주말에는 KTX 입석밖에 없을 때도 있어요.
On weekends there are sometimes only KTX standing tickets left.
입석(立席) = standing ticket; 밖에 + negative = 'nothing but'
nuance: KTX (Korea Train eXpress, spoken letter-by-letter as 케이티엑스) is the fast premium train Koreans set against three cheaper options: the 고속버스, the slower 무궁화호, and the mid-tier ITX-새마을. The boundary worth fixing is KTX vs SRT — both are bullet trains, but KTX is run by 코레일 (Korail) and SRT is a separate operator from 수서역, so the booking app differs. The signature English-speaker pitfall is reading the letters in English; a Korean always says 케이티엑스, sounding each letter Korean-style. A second trap is booking on the wrong app — for KTX you need 코레일톡, not the SRT app.

usage: the small step-through automatic motorbike; very common among delivery riders
the ones zipping around with food; 배달(配達) = delivery
you need a 원동기 or 2종 소형 license depending on engine size
legally required; 헬멧 안 쓰면 단속(團束) 대상 (subject to a crackdown)
examples: 저 사람은 스쿠터를 타요.
That person rides a scooter.
simple present habit; 타다 takes 을/를 for the vehicle you ride
스쿠터는 좁은 골목도 잘 다녀서 편해요.
Scooters get through narrow alleys well, so they're convenient.
다니다 = to get around/move about; explains why they're popular for delivery
비 올 때 스쿠터 타면 너무 위험해요.
Riding a scooter when it rains is really dangerous.
비(가) 오다 = to rain; a practical safety note residents make
nuance: 스쿠터 (from English 'scooter') means specifically the small automatic step-through motorbike with a seat and a low floorboard — the workhorse of food-delivery riders — whereas 오토바이 is the umbrella word for any motorcycle, including big manual-gear bikes. That contrast, 스쿠터 vs 오토바이, is the one to lock in: every 스쿠터 is an 오토바이, but most Koreans say 오토바이 generically and 스쿠터 only for the little delivery-style one. Crucially, do not confuse it with 전동킥보드, the standing electric kick-scooter with no seat that English also calls a 'scooter' — same English word, totally different vehicle in Korean. It collocates with 타다, 배달, 면허, 헬멧. The classic English-speaker pitfall is exactly that 'scooter' overlap (kick-scooter ≠ 스쿠터); a second is assuming no licence is needed — even a small 스쿠터 legally requires at least a 원동기 licence.

usage: 운전(運轉)하다 'operate/steer' is the standard verb for driving any vehicle
the small cargo truck everyone uses for moving; read '일 톤 트럭'
the truck a moving company brings; 이사(移徙) = moving house
대(臺) is the counter for vehicles and machines, never 개
examples: 저기 트럭이 한 대 있어요.
There's a truck over there.
introduces the vehicle counter 대; 한 대 = one (vehicle)
길에 트럭이 서 있어서 차가 막혀요.
A truck is parked on the road, so traffic is backed up.
서 있다 = to be standing/parked; 막히다 = (traffic) to be jammed
과일 파는 트럭이 동네에 자주 와요.
A truck selling fruit often comes to the neighborhood.
파는 (from 팔다) modifies 트럭; the 트럭 행상 street-vendor scene
nuance: 트럭 (from English 'truck') is everyday vocabulary mainly because of two very Korean sights: the 1톤 트럭 that families rent to move apartments, and the street vendors who sell fruit, vegetables, or fish straight off the back of one. There isn't a sharp single synonym, but note the register split — 트럭 is the ordinary spoken word, while 화물차(貨物車) 'cargo vehicle' is the more formal/official term you meet on road signs and in news. The counter is the trap that catches everyone: vehicles take 대 (트럭 한 대, 두 대), not the all-purpose 개, which would sound childish or wrong. It collocates with 운전하다, 빌리다, 1톤, 이사. The English-speaker pitfalls are (1) counting with 개 instead of 대, and (2) pronouncing it like one clipped English syllable — Korean breaks the consonant cluster with an inserted ㅡ vowel, so it is two clear syllables, 트·럭.

usage: 빌리다 = to rent/borrow, the standard verb here (the counter clerk's word is 대여하다)
예약(豫約)하다 'book in advance', done online before a trip, especially for 제주도
보험(保險) = insurance; always ask about 자차(自車) collision coverage
반납(返納) 'give back' = return; mind the fuel and time rules
examples: 여행 갈 때 렌터카를 빌려요.
When I go on a trip I rent a car.
simple habit sentence; 빌리다 takes 을/를 for the thing rented
렌터카 빌릴 때 면허증하고 신용카드가 필요해요.
When you rent a car you need your licence and a credit card.
practical requirement; 하고 links two nouns in speech
기름을 가득 채워서 반납해야 돼요.
You have to return it with a full tank.
가득 채우다 = to fill up; the common 만(滿)탱크 return rule
nuance: 렌터카 (from English 'rent-a-car') is the word residents reach for when a destination has weak public transport — above all 제주도, where almost every visitor rents. The boundary to keep clear is 렌터카 vs 카셰어링(car-sharing, e.g. 쏘카·그린카): a 렌터카 is a traditional desk-and-contract day-or-more rental, while 카셰어링 is the app-based by-the-minute/hour kind, so don't call a 쏘카 a 렌터카 in conversation. Spelling is a built-in trap because Koreans pronounce it 렌트카, yet the standardized loanword form is 렌터카 — write and read it with the 터. It collocates with 빌리다, 예약하다, 보험, 반납. The main English-speaker pitfalls are (1) writing/saying 렌트카 instead of 렌터카, and (2) forgetting the paperwork: you normally need a credit card in your own name plus a valid licence (an international permit if your home licence isn't recognized), and you'll always be pushed to add 보험 at the counter.

usage: Seoul's public bike-share; the name is deliberately cute/friendly
대여(貸與) = rental/checkout, done by app at a 대여소 (checkout point)
반납(返納) = return; you dock it at any 대여소 station
정기권(定期券) = a fixed-period pass (e.g. monthly), cheaper than paying per ride
examples: 주말에 따릉이를 타요.
I ride a Ttareungi on weekends.
simple habit; the brand name behaves like a normal object noun with 타다
지하철역까지 따릉이로 금방 가요.
I get to the subway station quickly by Ttareungi.
common last-mile use; 따릉이로 'by Ttareungi', 금방 = in no time
따릉이는 앱으로 잠금을 풀어요.
You unlock the Ttareungi with the app.
잠금을 풀다 = to release the lock/unlock; how the system works
nuance: 따릉이 is the brand name of Seoul's public bike-share, coined from the bicycle-bell sound 따르릉 plus the affectionate suffix -이, so the word literally evokes a cheerful 'ring-ring'. Because it is a proper brand, it is geographically specific to Seoul — other cities run their own systems with their own names (타슈 in Daejeon, 어울링 in Changwon, etc.), so 따릉이 ≠ '공공자전거' in general. The contrast to hold is 따릉이 (the rental/share brand) vs 자전거 (any bicycle, including your own): all 따릉이 are 자전거, but you only call it 따릉이 when it's one of these app-unlocked share bikes. It collocates with 타다, 대여/반납, 정기권, and 앱. The English-speaker pitfalls are (1) using 따릉이 for any bike — a personal bicycle is just 자전거 — and (2) assuming it exists nationwide, when outside Seoul you must look for the local equivalent.

usage: the standing share scooters from apps like 킥고잉, 씽씽
legally required; police run 단속(團束) crackdowns
you need at least a 원동기 licence to ride one legally
공유(共有) = shared; the app-based ones parked on sidewalks
examples: 요즘 전동킥보드를 많이 타요.
These days a lot of people ride electric kick-scooters.
simple frequency statement with 많이; 타다 + 을/를
전동킥보드는 헬멧을 안 쓰면 벌금을 내요.
If you don't wear a helmet on a kick-scooter, you pay a fine.
real rule since 2021; 벌금(罰金) = fine, 내다 = to pay
전동킥보드로 회사까지 십 분이면 가요.
I can get to work in ten minutes on a kick-scooter.
전동킥보드로 'by kick-scooter'; 십 분이면 = if it's (just) ten minutes
nuance: 전동킥보드 (電動 'electric-powered' + 킥보드 from English 'kickboard') is the standing electric scooter you push off and ride upright, and in real usage it almost always refers to the app-rented 공유 (shared) ones left scattered on sidewalks. The sharp contrast to drill is 전동킥보드 vs 스쿠터: a 전동킥보드 is a standing board with no seat, whereas a 스쿠터 is a seated, usually petrol step-through motorbike — English blurs both as 'scooter', which is exactly why learners mix them up. Note 킥보드 alone is the non-electric kid's kickboard; adding 전동 makes it the motorized adult share vehicle. It collocates with 타다, 헬멧, 면허, 공유, 벌금. The English-speaker pitfalls are (1) calling it a 스쿠터 because of the shared English word, and (2) assuming it's rule-free — riding two-up, without a helmet, or without a licence can each draw a 벌금.

usage: small green local buses that bridge gaps to the nearest subway station
정류장(停留場) 'stopping place' = bus stop; routes wind through the neighborhood
routes carry a district prefix plus a short number, like 종로11 or 강남07
환승(換乘) = transfer; you tap to transfer onward to the subway or a regular bus
examples: 집까지 마을버스를 타요.
I take the village bus to my house.
simple destination + 타다; 까지 marks the end point
마을버스는 작아서 출근 시간에 사람이 꽉 차요.
The village bus is small, so it's packed during commute hours.
꽉 차다 = to be packed full; 작아서 gives the reason
지하철에서 내려서 마을버스로 갈아타세요.
Get off the subway and transfer to the village bus.
갈아타다 = to change/transfer vehicles; common spoken directions
nuance: 마을버스 (마을 'village/neighborhood', native Korean, + 버스) is the small short-loop local bus that connects residential pockets — especially hilly ones away from main roads — to the nearest subway station or trunk bus line. The contrast to keep straight is 마을버스 vs 시내버스/광역버스: a 마을버스 only circles a small area as a feeder, a 시내버스 (city bus) runs longer routes across the city, and a 광역버스 connects cities, so don't expect a 마을버스 to take you far. Note 마을 is a pure-Korean word (not Sino-Korean), which is why it pairs warmly with the idea of a tight local community. It collocates with 타다, 정류장, 환승, 갈아타다, and route codes like 종로11. The English-speaker pitfalls are (1) expecting it to travel a long distance, when it only feeds bigger lines, and (2) forgetting to tap your card — without the tap the 환승 (free-transfer) discount to the subway won't apply.

mistakes: Expecting it to travel far — a 마을버스 only loops the local area to feed bigger lines, unlike a 시내버스 or 광역버스.
Forgetting to tap for transfer — without tapping your transport card, the 환승 (free-transfer) discount onto the subway won't apply.
Calling any small bus a 마을버스 — the term is the official route category (green, district-numbered), not just 'a little bus'.

usage: red express commuter buses linking Seoul with nearby cities like 수원, 일산
좌석(座席) = seat; these are seat-only and 입석 (standing) is restricted on them
노선(路線) = route/line; long commuter runs into the metro center
color-coded red, as opposed to blue (trunk) and green (local) city buses
examples: 회사까지 광역버스로 가요.
I go to work by wide-area bus.
simple commute statement; 광역버스로 'by wide-area bus', 까지 = up to
광역버스는 자리에 앉아서 갈 수 있어서 좋아요.
The wide-area bus is nice because you can sit the whole way.
-(으)ㄹ 수 있다 = can; the main appeal over a packed subway
출근 시간에는 광역버스가 만석이라 한 대 보냈어요.
At rush hour the wide-area bus was full, so I let one go by.
만석(滿席) = all seats taken; 한 대 보내다 = let one pass and wait
nuance: 광역버스 (廣域 'wide area' + 버스) is the red long-haul commuter bus that links Seoul with surrounding 경기도 cities, engineered so suburban commuters can sit for the whole ride into the center. The contrast you must fix is 광역버스 vs 마을버스: 광역버스 spans long city-to-city commutes and is seat-oriented, while 마을버스 just circles one neighborhood as a feeder — opposite ends of the bus spectrum. Korea's buses are also color-coded, and 광역버스 is the 빨간 (red) one, versus blue trunk and green local buses, so locals will say '빨간 버스' to mean it. It collocates with 타다, 좌석, 노선, 만석, and the verb 출근하다 (commute to work). The English-speaker pitfalls are (1) mixing it up with 마을버스 (wrong scale entirely) and (2) expecting to stand: because seats are limited and standing is restricted, a 만석 bus means you simply wait for the next one rather than squeezing on.

Expecting to stand on it — 광역버스 are largely seat-only with standing restricted, so when it's 만석 you wait for the next one.
Assuming all red buses are identical — color marks the category (red = 광역), but routes/노선 differ, so check the number.

usage: the gondola hung from a cable, up mountains or to coastal viewpoints
왕복(往復) 'go-and-return' = round trip; the opposite is 편도(片道) one way
표(票) = ticket; you buy it at the lower station
the lower station; -는 곳 = 'the place where you do (it)'
examples: 산에서 케이블카를 타요.
I ride the cable car on the mountain.
simple location + 타다; 에서 marks where the action happens
케이블카는 왕복으로 끊는 게 더 싸요.
Buying the cable car as a round trip is cheaper.
표를 끊다 = to buy a ticket (set idiom); 왕복으로 'as a round trip'
바람이 너무 세서 케이블카 운행을 멈췄어요.
The wind was too strong, so they stopped running the cable car.
운행(運行)을 멈추다 = to suspend operation; weather closures happen
nuance: 케이블카 (from English 'cable car') is leisure-and-tourism vocabulary — the gondola cabin that hangs from an overhead cable and carries you up 남산, 통영, or 여수 for the view, not for daily transport. The contrast to keep clear is by how it moves: a 케이블카 is suspended from a cable in the air, whereas a 모노레일 rides a single rail and a 트램 runs on tracks on the ground, so a ground-level car is not a 케이블카. Tickets pair it with the 왕복/편도 (round-trip / one-way) distinction, which directly affects price. It collocates with 타다, 왕복/편도, 표(를) 끊다, 야경, and 운행. The English-speaker pitfalls are (1) calling a ground tram or funicular a 케이블카 (those are 트램/모노레일 — 케이블카 hangs in the air), and (2) buying two 편도 tickets when a single 왕복 ticket is cheaper for an up-and-back trip.

Buying two 편도 tickets when a 왕복 ticket is cheaper for a there-and-back trip.

usage: the passenger/car ship to the islands; the formal term is 여객선(旅客船)
예매(豫買) = advance booking; popular island routes fill up
차량(車輛) = vehicle(s); the kind you can drive your car onto
터미널 = terminal; the port building you board from (also 여객터미널)
examples: 섬에 갈 때 페리를 타요.
I take a ferry when I go to the island.
core use case stated simply; 섬 = island, 타다 + 을/를
파도가 높아서 오늘 페리가 다 결항됐어요.
The waves are high, so all the ferries were canceled today.
결항(缺航)되다 = (a ship/flight) to be canceled; common in bad weather
페리에 차를 싣고 제주도에 갔어요.
I loaded my car onto the ferry and went to Jeju.
싣다 (ㄷ-irregular: 싣고/실어) = to load cargo; the car-ferry option
nuance: 페리 (from English 'ferry') is the everyday word for a passenger or car ship running point-to-point to Korea's islands; in formal notices and timetables you'll instead see the Sino-Korean 여객선(旅客船) 'traveler-guest ship', so 페리 ≈ 여객선 with 페리 being the casual term. The contrast to lock in is 페리 vs 유람선(遊覽船): a 페리 is transport that gets you from port A to island B, while a 유람선 is a sightseeing cruise that loops back to where it started — don't swap them. A practical companion word is 결항 (service cancellation), the thing you check before any island trip. It collocates with 타다, 예매, 차량, 터미널, and 결항. The English-speaker pitfalls are (1) calling a tour boat a 페리 (that's a 유람선), and (2) not checking the weather: rough seas trigger 결항, so an island ferry plan can collapse at the last minute.

Not checking the weather — rough seas cause 결항 (cancellation), so an island ferry plan can fall through last minute.
Treating 페리 as too casual for documents — official schedules and signage use 여객선, the formal equivalent.
